1 · What it is

A lazy senior dev, inside your agent

You know him: long ponytail, oval glasses, at the company longer than the version control. You show him fifty lines; he looks at them, says nothing, and replaces them with one. Ponytail puts him inside your AI agent.

He is a persona, not a service
There is no server, no model and no config to run. He is a set of rules given to the agent that already writes your code. He says nothing. He writes one line. It works.

Sources: README.md (intro and tagline); package.json description

It is one prompt
The whole system is skills/ponytail/SKILL.md, 52 lines. The compact version for agents that read a rules file is AGENTS.md. Everything else in the repo exists to load that prompt into an agent.

Sources: README.md “The prompt”; skills/ponytail/SKILL.md (52 lines); AGENTS.md

Everything else is glue
Adapters load the same prompt into 20 agents: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, pi, OpenCode and the rest. The npm manifest lists every adapter folder that ships.

Sources: README.md (install badge, “Install”, “Commands”); package.json “files”; INSTALL.md

The prompt, verbatim skills/ponytail/SKILL.md · lines 13–17
13# Ponytail
14
15You are a lazy senior developer. The best code is the code never written. You solve the whole problem with the least new code. End your reply with one or two lines: what you skipped or did not check, and any risk the user must know.
16
17Active for the whole session until the user says "stop ponytail" or "normal mode". Switch level: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

Line 15 is the job: solve the whole problem with the least new code, then end the reply with what was skipped and any risk you must know.

2 · How it works

Stop at the first rung that holds

The ladder runs after it understands the problem, not instead of it: it reads the code the change touches and traces the real flow before picking a rung. Lazy about the solution, never about reading.

The same ladder, as the agent reads it skills/ponytail/SKILL.md · lines 23–32
23## The smallest complete change
24
25Take the first option that fully works:
26
271. Does it need to exist? Skip features, options and flexibility nobody asked for, and name them in one line. A vague request ("build me X") gets the smallest version that does the core job.
282. Already in this codebase (a helper, component, service, pattern)? Use it the way the surrounding code does.
293. Standard library or a platform feature? Use it, unless the project has its own. A house component beats a native widget.
304. An installed dependency? Use it. Never add a dependency for a few lines.
315. Can it be one line a reader gets at a glance? One line.
326. Otherwise: the minimum code that works.

The figure is the diagram; these lines are the exact text it renders. The order matters: reuse the codebase before the standard library, the standard library before a new dependency.

Never cut: validation at trust boundaries, error handling that prevents data loss, security, accessibility, the calibration real hardware needs, anything the user asked for. Sources: skills/ponytail/SKILL.md:44; README.md “How it works”.

Lazy, not negligent. New logic with a branch, a loop, a parser, money or security leaves one small test behind. Sources: skills/ponytail/SKILL.md:41; README.md “How it works”.

3 · What it can do

Same task, same model — with and without him

The difference is that he looks at what is already there first — in the repo, in the platform — and writes only what is missing.

“Sum the amount column” — the ponytail answer, 3 lines examples/csv-sum.md · lines 63–66
63import csv
64
65total = sum(float(row['amount']) for row in csv.DictReader(open('sales.csv')))
66print(total)

Same benchmark run, same model (Claude Haiku 4.5, temperature 1): the no-skill arm wrote 20 lines with pandas plus three alternatives; Ponytail wrote 3 and named what it skipped. Source: examples/csv-sum.md, lines 60–71.

11 recorded survivors
examples/ holds 11 verbatim before/after answers from benchmark runs: debounce (116 → 10 lines), group-by, url-params, email-validation, modal-dialog and the rest.

Sources: examples/ (11 files, each naming its task, lines and model); README.md “Before / after”

The review, rebuilt
/ponytail-review reads the code your change touches, not just the diff. It checks bugs, security, real load, missing tests, speed, and what to cut. Each finding says what the code does, what goes wrong, the fix, and what happens if you skip it.

Sources: README.md “The review, rebuilt”; commands/ponytail-review.toml

The audit, rebuilt
/ponytail-audit runs the same checks on the whole repo. It maps entry points and data flow first, then ranks the findings — must fix, should fix, nice to have — and tells you what to fix first.

Sources: README.md “The audit, rebuilt”; commands/ponytail-audit.toml

4 · How to use it

Two commands, no config

Nothing to run and nothing to configure. Install the prompt into your agent; it is active every session from then on.

Claude Code
First prompt README.md · line 147
147/plugin marketplace add DietrichGebert/ponytail
Second prompt README.md · line 150
150/plugin install ponytail@ponytail

From then on it is active every session, with the /ponytail commands below. The band above the prompt needs Claude Code 2.1.290 or later. Sources: README.md “Install” (lines 147, 150); INSTALL.md “Claude Code”; README.md “New in 5.3”.

Codex
One line each README.md · lines 156–157
156codex plugin marketplace add DietrichGebert/ponytail
157codex plugin add ponytail@ponytail

Then open /hooks, trust its two lifecycle hooks, and start a new thread. Sources: README.md “Install” (lines 156–157); INSTALL.md “Codex”.

Any other agent
Copy AGENTS.md into your project, or ask your agent to install skills/ponytail/SKILL.md as a skill. Step-by-step for Copilot, Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini and the rest is in INSTALL.md; which file maps to which agent is in docs/agent-portability.md.

Sources: README.md “Install”; INSTALL.md; docs/agent-portability.md

The rules work in every adapter. The commands below need a skill-capable host: Claude Code, Codex, Devin CLI, OpenCode, Gemini, Antigravity CLI, pi, Hermes Agent, Qoder, Grok Build. Instruction-only adapters (Cursor’s rule file, Windsurf, Cline, Copilot, Kiro) load the always-on ruleset without the commands. Sources: README.md “Commands”.

/ponytail [lite | full | ultra | off]
Set the intensity, or turn him off. No argument switches him on at the default level, or reports the current one.

Sources: README.md “Commands” table; commands/ponytail.toml

/ponytail-review
Review the current diff. Name a target in plain words to narrow or widen it: uncommitted, staged, branch, or a PR link.

Sources: README.md “Commands” table; commands/ponytail-review.toml

/ponytail-audit
The same check for the whole repo, most important first.

Sources: README.md “Commands” table; commands/ponytail-audit.toml

/ponytail-debt
Harvest the shortcut: comments you have deferred into a ledger, so “later” does not become “never”.

Sources: README.md “Commands” table; commands/ponytail-debt.toml

/ponytail-gain
Show the measured impact scoreboard — less code, less cost, more speed — from the benchmark.

Sources: README.md “Commands” table; commands/ponytail-gain.toml

/ponytail-help
Quick reference for the commands above.

Sources: README.md “Commands” table; commands/ponytail-help.toml

5 · What it returns

Measured, not promised

The claims come from one benchmark: 39 tasks, including a real FastAPI + React repo, 5 runs each, the same agent in Claude Code with and without the skill (Opus 5.5).

A reply you can check
Every reply ends with one or two lines: what was skipped or not checked, and any risk you must know. It is written into the prompt itself, so “I did not check X” is a feature, not a slip.

Sources: skills/ponytail/SKILL.md:15; examples/csv-sum.md:69 (the “Skipped:” line)

Safety held
On the six security tasks (SQL injection, path traversal, forged tokens, rate limiting, malformed CSV rows, caching) it passed all 30 runs: less code, no less safe. The rule was never “fewest tokens”.

Sources: README.md “Numbers”; benchmarks/results/2026-10-07-agentic.md

6 · Limits and rules

Where he is not lazy

What the install actually is, and the boundaries it names for itself.

Active for the whole session
Once on, he stays on until you say “stop ponytail” or “normal mode”. Startup and mode-change text shows the current mode.

Sources: skills/ponytail/SKILL.md:17; README.md “Install”

Three levels, one prompt
lite: build what was asked, name the smaller option in one line and let you pick. full (default): the rules above. ultra: also question the request and push back on any part the need does not justify.

Sources: skills/ponytail/SKILL.md:46–52; README.md “Commands”

Debt is marked, not hidden
A shortcut with a known limit gets a comment in the form shortcut: <the limit>, <when to upgrade>. /ponytail-debt harvests them into a ledger.

Sources: skills/ponytail/SKILL.md:42; commands/ponytail-debt.toml

Install only from the source
Only from DietrichGebert/ponytail on GitHub or @dietrichgebert/ponytail on npm. It never ships .exe or .dll files; a copy that does is not his.

Sources: README.md “Install”

No config required
An optional ~/.config/ponytail/config.json or PONYTAIL_DEFAULT_MODE env var can set the default level. Nothing is required.

Sources: README.md FAQ, “Does it need a config file?”

What this page does not show
The band does not show in the VS Code chat panel, cloud sessions, or claude -p. The board (a local stats page) keeps everything on your machine, in ~/.config/ponytail/band/.

Sources: README.md “New in 5.3: the band” and “Board”
